items.title: The first DNA crime test didn’t catch the killer. It freed an innocent man.
items.summary: The events leading to the first forensic DNA case began in 1983. Lynda Mann was only 15 years old when, returning home from babysitting one evening in the Leicestershire village of Narborough, she was raped and murdered as she took a shortcut along a footpath known by villagers as the Black Pad. It was a path that would be unlikely to be known by anyone who wasn’t local, suggesting the killer was someone from the area. At the time, the biological side of forensic science was still in its infancy, though there were a handful of tests that could help narrow things down in terms of identifying the perpetrator. Investigators could determine from a semen sample that he was blood group A, which is the case for about 40% of the English population. Having established his blood group, they were able to tell that he was a “secretor,” which is true for about 70% of the population. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) enzyme testing was also carried out. PGM is an enzyme that both men and women carry, and it comes in a number of different forms; hence, determining which type the perpetrator had could also help narrow things down. The perpetrator was found to be type PGM1+, alongside around 40% of people with European ancestry living in England. As this combination of factors would be found in around 10% of all men, it was clearly not enough to identify the killer, though it would prove to be useful information a few years later. But for the time being, despite a huge police investigation, including door-to-door inquiries in Narborough and the nearby villages of Enderby and Littlethorpe, the trail eventually went cold. Then, in 1986, another young girl, Dawn Ashworth, was also raped and murdered just off another footpath, Ten Pound Lane, this time in Enderby, very close to Narborough. As in Lynda’s case, the killer’s modus operandi pointed to someone with local knowledge of the area: both the crimes took place in a part of each village that only locals were likely to know about. The similarities in both cases led the police to link the two crimes. There was a serial killer on the loose. Then came the first twist in the story, and with it, the first time that DNA “fingerprinting” would be used in a forensic case. Richard Buckland, a kitchen porter, aged 17 at the time and with learning difficulties, had been seen in the area on a motorbike, similar to the one that had been seen in the area when Dawn went missing. He also seemed to know, even before the police did, where Dawn might be found. The police brought him in and, under questioning, Richard confessed to Dawn’s murder, but he staunchly protested his innocence when it came to the second murder: He had not killed Lynda. With Richard in custody, the police were in a quandary. They were pretty convinced they had their suspect for both cases, but they needed new evidence to break the deadlock and also connect Richard to Lynda’s murder. The detective chief superintendent of the Leicestershire Police at the time, David Baker, had read an article in the local newspaper, the Leicester Mercury, about the work of [geneticist and DNA “fingerprinting” pioneer] Alec Jeffreys in the Sarbah case [of matching a mother and son’s DNA]. David had a brainwave. The police are always looking for new ways to help solve cases, and he recognized that this new technique could be used forensically: DNA fingerprinting could take this broad biological categorization of the perpetrator from being from a group of about 10% of the population, right down to “a group of one.” And if it could do that, it would confirm whether Richard Buckland had killed both girls, and he would go to jail for his crimes. In the meantime, Alec and his team were fine-tuning the DNA fingerprinting process. While the patterns of blobs and lines generated in the first version of DNA fingerprinting were ideal for telling individuals apart from one another, they were extremely complicated and difficult to explain in court. Alec’s team had been homing in on just some of these genetic stutters to understand more about them. They had been finding more and more of them across the genome, each following the same pattern — a DNA “word” repeated over and over again many times. It wasn’t the same word as before, however, but lots of different words, each of them tandemly repeated over and over again, and some were highly variable. There tends to be a standard range of repeats that you find in a population — say, between 10 and 27. So far from seeing only three possible combinations, the number of possible combinations was in the many hundreds for one marker alone. The team homed in on markers with considerable variation in the number of repeats an individual might have, making them perfect candidates for developing a more convenient test for casework. Concentrating on these markers, fine-tuning and polishing the technique, was starting to give what the forensic community, and courts, would want: something that was quick to carry out, easy to interpret (important when explaining things to a jury) but still highly specific in terms of telling individuals apart. It became known as DNA profiling. Alongside this, Alec had published a paper showing that DNA could be extracted not only from bloodstains up to four years old, but also from semen stains. In another breakthrough, it was now possible to separate sperm cells from vaginal cells and extract DNA from them; hence, DNA fingerprinting could be used to identify the perpetrator in a rape case. Each incremental scientific discovery was slowly leading towards the much-needed breakthrough in the hunt for Dawn and Lynda’s killer. Just as there was progress on the scientific front, so there was in the police investigation. Like Alec, David Baker could see the potential of linking DNA with forensics, and he was about to give Alec his first case. Between them, they would make history not once, but twice. DNA fingerprinting could take this broad biological categorization of the perpetrator from being from a group of about 10% of the population, right down to ‘a group of one.’ David’s request was simple. Convinced that there would be a DNA match, he asked Alec if he would run a DNA fingerprinting test on Richard Buckland and then on the samples taken from Lynda. A DNA match linking Richard to Lynda would provide the evidence linking him to her murder as well — both cases would be solved in one fell swoop. Alec agreed to run the test, and samples from Lynda and Richard Buckland were transferred to his lab just weeks later. This was to be his first ever forensic case and Alec was fully aware of the importance of what he was doing. Within a few days, he knew the DNA testing had worked, and he had his results. It was time to ring David with the news — both good and bad. The good news was that the DNA analysis had worked, but the bad news was that Richard Buckland’s DNA had not been found with Lynda’s. Lynda’s killer and Richard had completely different DNA fingerprints: The police had identified the wrong suspect for that murder. David then asked Alec to repeat the process with samples from Dawn. Again, the news was both good and bad: The DNA testing was successful, but it showed that, despite Richard’s confession, he hadn’t killed Dawn either. The young lad in custody was completely innocent of the crimes he was thought to have committed. On November 21, 1986, three years to the day since Lynda had been murdered, Richard Buckland was duly released. Thus the first time that DNA fingerprinting was used in a criminal case, rather than establishing the suspect’s guilt, as anticipated, it proved their innocence and exonerated them of a crime. items.title: I Need to Know How I Forgot I Wanted to Die
items.summary: What I Lost, What I Lose by Erica Dawson At my third ECT procedure, Tamara, a nurse, brought me warm blankets thin as sheets and inserted the catheter in my vein. She pushed Zofran for nausea, Toradol for pain, placed the scopolamine patch, for motion sickness, behind my left ear. The nurse anesthetist pushed a dose of caffeine equaling roughly eight cups of coffee in a few swallows. Caffeine lengthens the duration of the grand mal seizure, which is therapeutically beneficial, apparently, in combating treatment-resistant bipolar depression. So far, I wasn’t seizing long enough. I hadn’t had caffeine in months, for fear of it triggering mania. Here, in the hospital, the stimulant hit my blood and I started trembling so hard I got confused, in sheer panic, and thought they held the electrodes to my head, inducing the seizure while I was still awake. My heart rate increased and as the beeping from the pulse monitor became more and more urgent, I became convinced I was in cardiac arrest, about to flat line, and I wasn’t mad at that. They laid the gurney all the way down. Someone pressed on my shoulders, trying to minimize the shaking. I heard the doctor’s voice. Somebody said propofol . I woke up in the recovery room, disappointed, alive, still suicidal with a plan and intent, my voice cracking as I spoke to the nurse, asking for apple juice. Since having electroconvulsive therapy, I can’t remember parts of the past and, often, can’t make new memories. While I remember some moments from the hospital like this, I played the piano my whole life and now can’t read music. I studied Shakespeare to get a PhD and, the other day, had to look up the name of the guy who tricked Othello into murdering Desdemona. I can’t read long form writing; I can’t remember what happened in the previous pages. I don’t watch TV shows with several characters or complicated plots that play out over more than one episode. I spend a lot of time trying to goad my brain into recalling things I’ve lost and continued to lose on a daily basis. I look at photographs in my phone, ask people repetitive questions. I go down this road because, with a brain that oscillates between two extreme moods, I need the kind of stasis that comes from knowing where you’ve been or what you’ve done or what you can do. The exquisite hippocampus at its best. I can revisit having my head in Mom’s lap after ECT as she tried to massage the headaches out. I can remember rubbing my calves; it felt as if all 600 plus of my muscles hurt. I can go way back and tread through the grass of our old backyard, wrap my small hand around the swing set’s pole, lean back, and twirl. But out of 46 years of memories, what I need to know most is exactly how and when, during ECT, I stopped remembering I wanted to die. I’m not sure when I began considering ECT as an option to treat my bipolar depression. My doctor labeled me treatment-resistant a long time before. I tried all the meds. Mood stabilizers. Anticonvulsants. Antipsychotics. I underwent transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Nothing helped with the suicidality. I attended two partial hospitalization programs where, essentially, you’re admitted during the day for intensive care, support groups, and medication management, but allowed to go home at night. Every evening before I left the first program, in the exit assessment, a nurse would ask me if I had thoughts of harming myself. Each time, I answered yes . Placing the problems with the US healthcare system aside, I usually had the safety net of my mom at home. She flew from Maryland to Florida frequently, often for weeks at a time. She removed all sharp objects from the apartment, hid my medication, doling out only a single day’s pills. When she wasn’t in town, we’d FaceTime 24 hours straight and my medicine was kept at my best friend’s house. I checked in with my therapist every night, saw my psychiatrist once a week. With all those measures in place, I was safer than I would have been had I been on my own. Safer, but still wanting to die. I would find a way, eventually, to make it happen. Overdose on Benadryl, perhaps. Walk to the beauty supply and buy those sharp little eyebrow-trimming scissors. Already, I’d lost so much of myself to depression dulling my senses, replacing my personality with anhedonia. I’d think about my family. Especially my six-year-old nephew and my dog. My brother and sister-in-law just had to explain to my nephew what happened to Pop Pop, my dad who passed away less than a year earlier. And my dog? If we were alone when I went through with it, she, after, would be alone and confused. What would happen to her if EMTs or the police, and not my mom or a friend, got to her first? I hesitated. Torn between guilt and my suicidal urge, I thought I at least had to consider what I deemed my last resort. Desperate for something other than the life I was living—not much more than insomnia or somnolence, being bed-bound or pacing, occasionally taking the dog outside or sitting on my best friend’s stoop—I made an appointment with a psychiatrist, Dr. Woodson, who performed ECT, to see if I was a good candidate. He said I was. I’m pretty sure no one truly knows how electroconvulsive therapy works, but people swear by it. Patients, doctors, scientists. Possibly, the seizure helps release neurotransmitters which alter brain chemistry, relieving symptoms of depression. Or, the seizure permanently changes neural pathways. Before my appointment with Dr. Woodson, I skimmed a memoir where the author described how their depression, after ECT, had completely disappeared. I got most of my information from the ECT scenes in One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest and Requiem for a Dream , where Jack Nicholson’s Randle and Ellen Burstyn’s Sara absorb the electricity and seize without general anesthesia. I knew enough to know the use of general anesthesia was standard now and had been since the 1960s. And I did know about the procedure’s potential problems, too. But the side effects , Mom said. Dr. Woodson clearly laid out what he called slight possibilities for memory loss and cognitive impairment. He said the memory loss usually was contained to the time during which you received the treatment. Those memories will likely come back , he assured me. Slight. Usually . Likely . Already, I’d lost so much of myself to depression dulling my senses, replacing my personality with anhedonia. Other than the desire to kill myself, I had no real desires, no strong opinions. I felt as if I had nothing to look forward to. I hardly had the energy to think. Impaired cognition wouldn’t be unfamiliar. At this point I couldn’t work. What started as an illness morphed into disability. Black, female, and disabled: a minority three times over which likely wouldn’t help me find any sense of autonomy amidst my ailing confidence. I thought: Could things really get much worse? I’d already left the Erica I knew behind years ago when the severe depression settled in. Now I faced the hardest decision I’d ever make. Maybe lose even more of who I was but possibly have a chance at survival or, sooner than later, at my own hand, die . I scheduled my first ECT treatment for Monday, April 4, 2022. I can’t remember the specific consent documents, but I’ve looked at several examples online, all basically the same. Confusion can result but generally clears in an hour. Retrograde memory loss sometimes goes back one, two, or more years. For a brief period, difficulty with aspects of learning and thinking, in addition to anterograde amnesia (making new memories) can happen. The risk of death is very low. And there’s always something like this: Reports show some people have memory problems and cognitive impairment much more serious and long-lasting. items.title: Exclusive Cover Reveal of SHAMEWRECK by Peggy Shinner
items.summary: Electric Literature is pleased to reveal the cover of Shamewreck by Peggy Shinner, which will be published on February 9, 2027 by Mad Creek Books. You can pre-order your copy here . For readers of Eula Biss and Cathy Park Hong, essays that knit cultural criticism, social history, and personal experience to excavate the entanglements of shame, power, language, and identity. In Shamewreck , Peggy Shinner interrogates the entanglement of shame and language, casting shame as a moral force, a conscience-beast, an umpire, the fellow who awaits when you come home. These essays grapple with the nuclear bombing of Bikini Atoll and the emergence, four days later, of the bikini in Paris; the link between property and personhood and what it means to die without possessions; the mutability of language and how shamefaced once meant “modest and bashful,” before morphing into the opposite, “abashed and ashamed”; how talkative women were thought to be sloppy women, like Eve (loose of mouth and morals); how occupation once meant “heterosexual intercourse” and now means “military invasion.” Parsing the dark undercurrents of popular culture alongside her own experiences as a queer woman, Shinner exhorts us to abandon willful unseeing and consider the legacies of language. Take a look, she urges, you can buy a new car in 21st century America and for your money get two masters and a slave key. Shamewreck complicates our notions of shame and shamelessness and rescues them from the refuse pile, reclaiming shame as a potent moral adjudicator. Here is the cover, designed by Charles Brock: Peggy Shinner: Shamewreck is, in many ways, an invitation to look at the unsightly or, to put it another way, the unseen, and make it visible. What would such a book look like? There were three elements I was sure of: strong type, saturated color, and no human figures. I wanted to steer clear of the tired visual tropes of shame: head bowed, shoulders slumped, gaze averted. So I had a feel for the cover, but not a specific image. At the last minute I sent my editor a photo of a bombed US naval ship at Bikini Atoll, referencing one of the essays in the book. An actual, irradiated shipwreck. Then the prestidigitation, out of sight, out of my sight, happened. Soon the cover arrived. Not the ship I sent but another ship, on its side, mostly submerged, nose up and precariously tilted, heading toward the bottom, completely unanchored. Then and now I was astounded. I love the cover for its somewhat queasy green color (shame can be queasy-making); the visual and aural rhyming of shipwreck/shamewreck, both ship and shame upended; the water, too, upended, along the whole length of the spine; the horizontal bands of deep purple, the encapsulated lowercase typography in an astonishing pink, an explosion of color and the centerpiece, pinning it all down. The whole disturbing disturbance. I’m grateful to Charles Brock for his vision and his palette and how the cover surprises me every time I look at it. Charles Brock: A shipwreck was suggested as a possible image for the cover. There was concern that the cover might look like a history book with a ship on the cover. So the choice was made to rotate the image and use a halftone effect so that it had more of a graphic feel as opposed to a photo. The author likes strong type. I took Barbara Kruger as inspiration and used Futura Bold Oblique for the cover type. I think the graphic treatment on the image, combined with the bold type and unconventional colors work well to communicate that Shamewreck is not a history book. items.title: 3 original methods for measuring the distance to the stars
items.summary: Out there in space, blazing just a scant 150 million kilometers away lies the brightest and most massive object in our Solar System: the Sun. Shining hundreds of thousands of times as bright in Earth’s skies as the next brightest object, the full Moon, the Sun is unique among Solar System objects for producing its own visible light, rather than only appearing illuminated because of reflected light. However, the thousands upon thousands of stars visible in the night sky — escalating into the millions and billions when we aid our vision with telescopes and cameras — are all also self-luminous, distinguishing themselves from the planets and other Solar System objects in that regard. But how far away are they? Unlike the planets, Sun, and Moon, the stars appear to remain fixed in their position over time: not only from night-to-night but also throughout the year and even from year-to-year. We even call it “the fixed background of stars” when measuring the motion of objects within our Solar System against them. Compared to the objects in our own Solar System, the stars must be incredibly far away. And therefore, in order to be seen from such great distances, they must be incredibly intrinsically bright. It only makes sense to assume, as many did dating back to antiquity, that those stars must be Sun-like objects located at great distances from us. But how far away are they? It wasn’t until the 1600s that we got our first answers, one each from three titans of physics history: Robert Hooke, Christiaan Huygens, and Isaac Newton. Unsurprisingly, those early answers didn’t agree with one another, but who came closest to getting it correct, and whose methods helped us the most in the centuries to come? The story is as educational as it is fascinating. The stars that are closest to Earth will appear to shift periodically with respect to the more distant stars as the Earth moves through space in orbit around the Sun. Before the heliocentric model was established, we weren’t looking for “shifts” with a ~300,000,000 kilometer baseline over the span of ~6 months, but rather a ~12,000 kilometer baseline over the span of one night: Earth’s diameter as it rotated on its axis. The distances to the stars are so great that it wasn’t until the 1830s that the first parallax, with a 300 million km baseline, was detected. Today, we’ve measured the parallax of over 1 billion stars with ESA’s Gaia mission. Credit : ESA/ATG medialab The first method: Robert Hooke The simplest, most straightforward and direct way to measure the distances to the stars is one that dates back thousands of years: the notion of stellar parallax. The idea is the same one as the phenomenon behind the game we all play as children, where you: close one eye, hold your thumb up at arm’s length from you, then switch which eye is closed and which one is open, and watch your thumb shift relative to the objects farther away in the background. Whenever you have two different vantage points to look from (such as each of your two eyes), objects that are close by will appear to “shift” relative to the objects that are farther away. This phenomenon, known as parallax, could theoretically be used to measure the distances to any of the stars, but would be most easily leveraged for the closest stars of all. At least, that would be true under the assumption that the stars are actually close enough to appear to shift, given the limitations of our bodies, our equipment, and our vantage point. In ancient times, people assumed that the cosmos was geocentric, so they attempted to observe parallax by looking at the same stars at dawn and at dusk, seeing if a baseline distance of one Earth diameter (as the Earth rotates over that 12 hour span) between the two observing points would lead to an observable shift in any stars. As it turns out, no such shift is detectable. However, in the 1600s, after the work of Copernicus, Galileo, and Kepler revealed a heliocentric model to our Universe, scientist Robert Hooke thought the parallax method might now at last bear fruit. This drawing shows Robert Hooke’s zenith telescope, constructed in the late 1660s and used to attempt to measure the position of the zenith star at his location, Gamma Draconis, and any variations in its position with respect to a plumb line, which would indicate a stellar parallax. Credit : R. Hooke, An Attempt to Prove the Motions of Earth by Observations, 1674 In the late 1660s, Hooke went for it. He knew that atmospheric refraction (or the bending of light rays due to Earth’s atmosphere) might be a problem, so to minimize that effect, he built what’s known as a zenith telescope: a telescope that looked straight up overhead, minimizing the amount of Earth’s atmosphere that light would need to travel through. Measuring the position of Gamma Draconis — the zenith star as visible from his location in London, England — Hooke took multiple observations of the star over the course of the year, looking for any apparent shift in its position from “true zenith,” to the best precision his instruments could muster. He recorded four measurements beginning in 1669, and noticed a variation that he claimed was observable with the precision of his instruments: 25 arc-seconds, or about 0.007 degrees. He published his results in An Attempt to Prove the Motions of Earth by Observations in 1674, wherein he wrote: “Tis manifest then by the observations … that there is a sensible parallax of Earth’s Orb to the fixt Star in the head of Draco, and consequently a confirmation of the Copernican System against the Ptolomaick [Ptolemaic] and Tichonick [Tychonic].” The inferred distance to Gamma Draconis, according to Hooke’s measurements, would work out to about 0.26 light-years, or 16,500 times the Earth-Sun distance. When compared against the modern result, it turns out that Hooke’s measurements were way off; Gamma Draconis is actually 154 light-years away and has a parallax of only 21 milli -arc-seconds, or over a factor of 1000 smaller than Hooke’s measurement. The way that light spreads out as a function of distance means that the farther away from a power source you are, the energy that you intercept drops off as one over the distance squared. This also illustrates, if you view a certain specific angular area (illustrated by the squares) from the perspective of the original source, how larger objects at greater distances will appear to take up the same angular size in the sky. Each time you double your distance between a source and observer, the brightness you observe gets quartered. In general, photons (and all light) propagate spherically outward away from the emitting source. Credit : Borb/Wikimedia Commons The second method: Christiaan Huygens Many astronomers, throughout the 17th century and even earlier, had a very different idea for how to estimate the distances to the stars. First, you assume that the Sun is a typical star, with a typical intrinsic brightness and size. Then, you measure the relative brightness of the Sun compared to the observed brightness of a star in the night sky. And finally, you use the fact that brightness falls off as one-over-the-distance-squared (an inverse square law, as shown above) to calculate how much farther away those stars are than the Sun is. The problem that everyone who attempted to leverage such a method faced, however, was the difficulty of that second step. Given that the Sun is so incredibly bright and the stars — even the brightest among them — are so incredibly faint, a fair comparison seemed practically impossible. Beyond that, you can only see the stars at night, when the Sun has set, so a side-by-side, simultaneous comparison is practically impossible. That’s where Huygens came in.
